title: Black Holes: The Universe's Dark Mystery
author: ReadingPlanet Staff
summary: Explore the fascinating science of black holes and what happens when stars die.

vocabulary.definition: the force that attracts objects toward each other, especially the force that makes things fall to the ground
vocabulary.sentence: Black holes have such strong gravity that nothing can escape, not even light.

vocabulary.definition: an explosion of a star that briefly outshines an entire galaxy
vocabulary.sentence: When a massive star dies in a supernova, it can leave behind a black hole.

vocabulary.definition: in black hole science, the boundary beyond which nothing can escape
vocabulary.sentence: Once something crosses the event horizon of a black hole, it can never return.

content.text: Imagine something so powerful that even light cannot escape from it. That is a black hole. These mysterious objects are some of the most fascinating phenomena in the universe. Scientists have studied them for decades, and we are still learning new things about them.

Most black holes form when massive stars die. Stars are powered by nuclear fusion in their cores, which pushes outward against gravity. When a star runs out of fuel, gravity wins. The star collapses inward with tremendous force. If the star is massive enough, it keeps collapsing until it becomes a black hole.

This collapse happens in a violent explosion called a supernova. The outer layers of the star blast outward into space. Meanwhile, the core crushes down into an incredibly small, dense point. A black hole the mass of our sun would be only about four miles across.

Every black hole has an invisible boundary called the event horizon. This is the point of no return. Anything that crosses the event horizon is trapped forever. Light, matter, information - nothing escapes. From outside, you cannot see what is inside a black hole.

The gravity at the event horizon is unimaginably strong. If you fell toward a black hole feet first, gravity would pull harder on your feet than your head. You would be stretched like spaghetti. Scientists actually call this process spaghettification.

Since black holes are invisible, how do scientists find them? They look for their effects on nearby matter. Gas and dust falling into a black hole heat up and glow brightly. Stars orbiting close to black holes move in unusual ways. By studying these clues, astronomers can locate black holes.

In 2019, scientists captured the first image of a black hole. It showed the shadow of a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy. This black hole is 6.5 billion times more massive than our sun. The image was created by linking telescopes around the world.

Scientists believe there is a supermassive black hole at the center of our own Milky Way galaxy. It is called Sagittarius A* and is about four million times the mass of our sun. Thankfully, it is 26,000 light-years away - far too distant to pose any danger to Earth.

comprehension.question: What causes most black holes to form?
options: The death and collapse of massive stars
Collisions between galaxies
Explosions in empty space
The cooling of hot gas clouds

comprehension.question: Why is the event horizon called 'the point of no return'?
options: Because time moves backward there
Because nothing that crosses it can escape
Because it is visible from Earth
Because it marks the center of the black hole

comprehension.question: What is 'spaghettification'?
options: A type of Italian food served in space
The stretching effect caused by extreme gravity
How black holes spin
The color of black holes

options: By sending a spacecraft to photograph it
By linking telescopes around the world
By using a satellite in orbit
By studying old photographs
